Series::nanstd¶

Back to SeriesStatAccessor API Reference

Signature¶

Series::nanstd() const -> Series
Series::nanstd(std::int64_t dim) const -> Series
Series::nanstd(std::int64_t dim, bool keepdim) const -> Series
Series::stat.nanstd(...) -> Series
Series::stat().nanstd(...) -> Series

What It Does¶

nanstd() is the standard-deviation companion to nanvar().

It keeps the same missing-data rule:

  • ignore NaNs

  • compute over the observed values that remain

  • use the population convention

The main difference is interpretability. nanstd() reports spread in the same units as the input, so it is often easier to read directly than nanvar().

Like nanvar(), there is no unbiased toggle here. This method always uses the NaN-omitting population convention.

Overload Map¶

nanstd()

Global NaN-omitting population standard deviation.

nanstd(dim)

Axis-wise NaN-omitting population standard deviation.

nanstd(dim, keepdim)

Axis-wise NaN-omitting population standard deviation with optional axis retention.

stat.nanstd(...) / stat().nanstd(...)

Accessor spellings for the same reduction family.

Parameters¶

dim (std::int64_t)

The axis to reduce.

  • positive dims count from the front

  • negative dims count from the back

  • the dim must exist

keepdim (bool, default false)

Whether the reduced axis stays in the result shape as size 1.

Returns¶

Series A floating-point NaN-omitting population standard deviation result.

Gradient¶

nanstd() is primarily a descriptive reduction with explicit missing-data policy.

Use it when omission is semantically correct, not because you want NaNs to quietly disappear from every analysis step.

Examples¶

These examples deliberately contrast nanstd() with ordinary std() so the policy difference is impossible to miss.

Example 1. Global nanstd() ignores NaNs and computes over the observed population.

auto missing = pluss::make_series({
    {1.0, std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN(), 3.0},
    {std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN(), 5.0, 7.0},
});

std::cout << missing.nanstd();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=2.236068

Example 2. nanstd(0) makes the one-observed-value rule visible in standard deviation form.

std::cout << missing.nanstd(0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0, 2]

Columns 0 and 1 each have one observed value, so their standard deviation is 0.

Example 3. nanstd(1) computes one NaN-omitting population standard deviation per row.

std::cout << missing.nanstd(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 1]

Example 4. keepdim=true preserves the reduced axis.

std::cout << missing.stat.nanstd(-1, true);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,1], strides=[1,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[[1],
  [1]]

For rank 2, -1 means the last axis, so this is row-wise nanstd() with axis retention.

Example 5. The explicit proxy spelling gives the same result.

std::cout << missing.stat().nanstd(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 1]

Example 6. std() and nanstd() answer different questions on the same data.

std::cout << missing.std(1, false) << "\n";
std::cout << missing.nanstd(1) << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[nan, nan]
pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 1]

This contrast is the heart of the API split:

  • std() propagates NaNs

  • nanstd() omits them

Example 7. An all-NaN lane still has no observed spread, so the result is NaN.

auto none = pluss::make_series({
    std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN(),
    std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN(),
});

std::cout << none.nanstd();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=nan

Example 8. Invalid dims fail explicitly, but the current message reuses nanvar wording.

try {
  std::cout << missing.nanstd(2) << "\n";
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n')) << "\n";
}

Output¶

nanvar: dim out of range

That is a real current quirk worth documenting honestly.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • nanstd() always uses the population convention.

  • One observed value yields 0.

  • All-NaN lanes yield NaN.

  • nanstd() and std() differ by policy, not just convenience.

  • Some current nanstd(...) dim failures report through nanvar wording.

Summary¶

Use nanstd() when NaN means “missing value that should be ignored during the reduction” and you want spread in the original units.

  • Choose it instead of std() when omission is the correct policy.

  • Expect singleton observed lanes to return 0.

  • Expect all-NaN lanes to remain undefined and return NaN.

  • Keep the axis with keepdim=true when downstream shape alignment matters.

The key question to ask is not “do I want standard deviation?” but rather “what should NaN mean in this analysis?”

See Also¶

  • Series::nanvar: squared spread with the same omission rule.

  • Series::std: ordinary standard deviation that propagates NaNs.
